title: Countability and Quantifiers
summary: Which nouns can be counted in English, how to quantify the ones that cannot, and which quantifier fits which noun.

sections.heading: Nouns that are uncountable in English
sections.body:
A set of very common academic nouns is **uncountable** in English although the equivalent word is countable in Arabic and in many European languages: `information`, `advice`, `research`, `evidence`, `equipment`, `furniture`, `knowledge`, `progress`, `staff`, `news`, `luggage`, `work`, `feedback`, `traffic`, `homework`.

An uncountable noun takes **no plural -s** and **no `a/an`**, and it takes a singular verb. `Informations`, `an advice`, `many researches` and `two equipments` are not options in careful English, however natural they feel.

examples.right: The supervisor gave me some useful advice about structuring the review.
examples.wrong: The supervisor gave me some useful advices about structuring the review.

examples.right: Recent research suggests that sleep consolidates memory.
examples.wrong: Recent researches suggest that sleep consolidates memory.
examples.note: `Research` is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

examples.right: The news from the ministry was worse than expected.
examples.wrong: The news from the ministry were worse than expected.
examples.note: `News` looks plural but is uncountable and singular.

sections.heading: Partitives: how to count the uncountable
sections.body:
When a single unit really is needed, English inserts a **partitive** — a countable measure word — before `of`: `a piece of advice`, `an item of equipment`, `a body of research`, `a bit of information`, `a word of warning`, `a great deal of progress`.

The partitive is what carries the plural: `three pieces of equipment`, `several items of furniture`. Some partitives are collocationally fixed: research comes in `a body of`, evidence in `a body of` or `a piece of`, and luggage in `an item of`.

examples.right: The laboratory ordered three new items of equipment.
examples.wrong: The laboratory ordered three new equipments.
examples.note: The partitive noun takes the plural, not the uncountable noun.

examples.right: A growing body of research links air quality to cognitive performance.
examples.wrong: A growing number of researches link air quality to cognitive performance.
examples.note: `A body of research` is the standard academic partitive.

examples.right: Let me give you one piece of advice before the interview.
examples.note: `A piece of` supplies the countability that `advice` lacks.

sections.heading: Nouns that switch, and what changes
sections.body:
A number of nouns are uncountable in one sense and countable in another, and the change is a change of **meaning**, not merely of form.

`Experience` uncountable is accumulated skill (`ten years of experience`); `experiences` countable are individual events (`her experiences abroad`). `Time` uncountable is duration (`we have no time`); `times` countable are occasions (`three times`). `Paper` uncountable is the material; `papers` are articles or documents. `Work` uncountable is labour; `works` are creative or engineering constructions. `Business` uncountable is commerce; `a business` is a company.

examples.right: The internship gave her practical experience of laboratory work.
examples.wrong: The internship gave her practical experiences of laboratory work.

examples.right: She presented two papers at the conference and printed them on recycled paper.
examples.note: The same word, countable as an article and uncountable as a material.

examples.right: There is not enough time, and I have asked them three times already.

sections.heading: Much, many, little, few, less, fewer
sections.body:
`Much` and `little` go with uncountable nouns; `many` and `few` with plurals. In affirmative statements `much` sounds formal and is usually replaced by **a great deal of**, **a large amount of** or **plenty of**, while `many` survives more easily; in questions and negatives both are natural (`How much progress?`, `not many students`).

The indefinite article reverses the tone. `A few` and `a little` are positive and mean *some, enough*; `few` and `little` are negative and mean *hardly any*. `She has a few friends here` is reassuring; `She has few friends here` is not.

**Fewer** is used with countables and **less** with uncountables (`fewer bags`, `less plastic`), and the same split governs **number of** for countables and **amount of** for uncountables.

examples.right: Supermarkets now issue fewer plastic bags than they did a decade ago.
examples.wrong: Supermarkets now issue less plastic bags than they did a decade ago.

examples.right: The number of applications has risen, although the amount of funding has not.
examples.wrong: The amount of applications has risen, although the number of funding has not.
examples.note: `Number of` for countables, `amount of` for uncountables.

examples.right: She has a few contacts in the department, so she rarely feels isolated.
examples.wrong: She has few contacts in the department, so she rarely feels isolated.
examples.note: Without `a`, `few` means hardly any, which contradicts the second clause.

examples.right: The team made a great deal of progress in the first month.
examples.wrong: The team made many progress in the first month.
examples.note: `Progress` is uncountable; `a great deal of` is the natural affirmative quantifier.

sections.heading: Some and any
sections.body:
The default division is that **some** belongs to affirmative statements and **any** to negatives and questions: `There is some information on the site` / `There isn't any information on the site` / `Is there any information on the site?`

The exception matters in speech: `some` is used in questions that are **offers or requests**, because the speaker expects a yes. `Would you like some coffee?` and `Could you give me some help?` are offers, not genuine enquiries.

`Any` also appears in affirmative sentences with the meaning *it does not matter which*: `Any student may apply`.

examples.right: Would you like some coffee before the session starts?
examples.wrong: Would you like any coffee before the session starts?
examples.note: An offer takes `some`, since a yes is anticipated.

examples.right: There isn't any information on the website about the entry requirements.
examples.wrong: There isn't some information on the website about the entry requirements.

examples.right: Any applicant with a relevant degree is eligible.
examples.note: Affirmative `any` meaning it makes no difference which.

sections.heading: Each, every, all, both, either, neither
sections.body:
These differ in the **noun form** and the **verb form** they require. `Each` and `every` take a singular noun and a singular verb (`each student was interviewed`, `every proposal has merit`); `each` can also stand after `of` with a plural (`each of the students was interviewed`). `Either` and `neither` likewise take a singular noun and, in careful writing, a singular verb.

`Both` and `all` take plurals — `both proposals`, `all students` — except that `all` also combines with uncountables (`all evidence`). `None of` is followed by a plural or uncountable noun and, in formal writing, a singular verb.

Note that `every` refers to the group as a whole and `each` to the members one at a time, and that `neither` is used only of two items; for more than two, use `none`.

examples.right: Each candidate was interviewed separately, and all of them received written feedback.
examples.note: `Each` takes a singular noun and a singular verb.

examples.right: Neither of the two proposals addresses the underlying problem.
examples.wrong: Neither of the two proposals address the underlying problem.
examples.note: `Neither` is grammatically singular in careful writing.

examples.right: Both methods produced the same result, but neither was cheap.
examples.wrong: Both method produced the same result.

slips: Pluralising an English uncountable: `informations`, `advices`, `researches`, `equipments`, `furnitures`. These words have no plural, whatever their equivalents do in Arabic.
Writing `an advice` or `a research`. Use a partitive instead: `a piece of advice`, `a body of research`.
Using `less` with a countable noun (`less students`, `less bags`). Countables take `fewer`.
Saying `the amount of students`. Countables take `the number of`; only uncountables take `the amount of`.
Dropping the `a` in `a few` or `a little` and reversing the meaning: `few results` says hardly any, not some.
Treating `staff`, `news` or `progress` as plural: `the staff is` or `the staff are` is a real choice, but `staffs` and `newses` are not.

questions.prompt: The supervisor gave me ___ on how to structure the literature review.
questions.explain: `Advice` is uncountable, so it takes neither a plural -s nor `a`. The countable-looking forms would need a partitive: `a useful piece of advice`.

questions.prompt: Let me give you one useful ___ of advice before the interview.
questions.explain: An uncountable noun is counted through a partitive: a piece, a bit or a word of advice. The partitive carries the number, not `advice` itself.

questions.prompt: Supermarkets now issue ___ plastic bags than they did a decade ago.
questions.explain: `Bags` is countable, so the comparative is `fewer`. `Less` is common on signage but belongs with uncountables such as `less plastic`.

questions.prompt: The ___ of students enrolling in online courses has risen sharply since 2020.
questions.explain: Countable nouns take `the number of`; `the amount of` is reserved for uncountables such as funding or time.

questions.prompt: She has ___ contacts in the department, so she rarely feels isolated at work.
questions.explain: `A few` means some, enough; bare `few` means hardly any and would contradict the second clause.

questions.prompt: He speaks with authority because he has ___ experience of teaching abroad.
questions.explain: `Experience` in the sense of accumulated skill is uncountable, so it takes `a great deal of`. The `number` phrases require a plural countable noun.

questions.prompt: Would you like ___ coffee before the afternoon session begins?
questions.explain: Questions normally take `any`, but an offer or request takes `some` because the speaker anticipates a yes.

questions.prompt: ___ of the two proposals addresses the underlying funding problem; both assume the grant will be renewed.
questions.explain: `Neither` negates two alternatives and takes a singular verb. `None` is used of three or more, and `Either` would assert that one of them does address the problem.

questions.prompt: The placement year gave her practical ___ of laboratory work.
questions.explain: Uncountable `experience` is accumulated skill. Countable `experiences` would mean separate memorable events, which does not fit `practical ... of laboratory work`.

questions.prompt: How ___ progress have you made on the first draft?
questions.explain: `Progress` is uncountable, so the question word is `much`. `Many` would require a plural countable noun.

questions.prompt: Sadly, ___ evidence was found to support the hypothesis, and the project was abandoned.
questions.explain: `Evidence` is uncountable, which rules out `few` and `a few`, and the negative outcome calls for `little` rather than the positive `a little`.

questions.prompt: There isn't ___ information on the website about the entry requirements.
questions.explain: Negative statements take `any`; `some` belongs in affirmatives and in offers.
